newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF may defend franc but rate rise seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: BoF may defend franc but rate rise seen unlikely.

text.p: The Bank of France is unlikely to raise interest rates to defend the franc ahead of likely snap elections, but has plenty of marks in its reserves to intervene on currency markets if necessary, economists said on Monday.
Seven economists polled by Reuters said they did not expect the Bank to raise rates -- a move it has often made in previous times of political instability.

The franc, they said, was unlikely to slide dramatically, and in any case the central bank had hefty reserves to stem any decline after buying marks heavily in recent months to prevent too great a surge in the French currency.

"The Bank of France has a lot of reserves in marks, and can sell them to buy francs. If that proved insufficient, the Bundesbank could step in, first by issuing statements and then by buying francs," Banques Populaires economist Jean-Martial Breuil said.

Banque Internationale de Placement economist Marie Owens-Thomsen said she expected the Bank to intervene to head off any risk of the franc falling through 3.4293 per mark, its floor in the former 2.25 percent narrow bands of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.
"They can defend it. They have plenty of reserves now too. They have got plenty of marks," she said. The franc was trading on Monday at around 3.3770 per mark.
"They have been intervening to support the mark against the franc quite a lot since the beginning of the year. They have plenty of cash to intervene," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.

Economists explained their belief that the franc would not in any case fall too sharply in different ways, with some saying a victory by the opposition Socialists would not change policy too much and others betting on a renewal of the centre-right majority.

Both main left and right political groupings say they are committed to European monetary union and President Jacques Chirac would continue to control foreign -- and therefore European policy -- regardless of which side wins.
"I see no reason for the franc to fall, this is but a short-term political uncertainty," said Martine Aubert at Credit Commercial de France.

"Even if the political opposition won the election, it would not affect economic policy very much," Jean-Louis Mourier at Louis Dreyfus Finance added. Sonja Gibbs at Nomura said she thought the franc would not plunge dramatically, "because...people know Chirac will keep a working majority."
"There is no trust in Socialists in France right now. And it is not foreign investors who own francs but domestics, and they will not lose confidence," she added.
"Jacques Chirac would only take such a decision (to hold early elections) in view of favourable polls, he must expect to keep a working majority," Francois Chevallier at BFCE said.

All economists said they did not expect the Bank to cut rates in the near term, though they said that in the longer term it had room to shave its key intervention rate, now at 3.10 percent, by 10 basis points to match the German repo rate.
Chirac was expected to announce early elections in a televised address due at 1800 GMT.
